title: Lab 7: Introducing the t-statistic
text:
In this lab, we’ll learn about the t-statistic and how it can be used to test a hypothesis, specifically using a one-sample t-test. Before starting this lab, make sure to have read Chapter 7: t Tests: An Introduction to Comparing Two Things from your textbook.






NoteLearning objectives



By the end of this lab, you should be able to:

Understand the basic properties of the t distribution
Define what degrees of freedom are
Understand the differences between a z and t distribution
Use R to conduct and interpret the output of a one-sample t-test
Report the output of a one-sample t-test using APA formatting

title: Lab 7: Introducing the t-statistic
text:
The t-distribution
Luckily for us, we can address this by using a slightly different distribution, called the t-distribution. Just like our standard normal distribution (i.e., the z-distribution), the t-distribution tells us the complete set of t-values calculated for every possible random sample of a given size.
One of the key differences is that our t-distribution is a family of distributions that differ based on the sample size. Specifically, we will have a different t-distribution for every number of degrees of freedom (df). The degrees of freedom tells us the number of observations that are free to vary when estimating a parameter. Every time that we estimate a parameter in our population, we introduce a constraint onto our data. When estimating our population standard deviation, the associated calculation for degrees of freedom is \(df=n-1\). However, note that there are different ways of calculating degrees of freedom depending on the situation.
The image below provides an illustration of how the t-distribution changes with different degrees of freedom. In addition, you can see how t-distributions compare to the standard normal distribution. To see the t-distribution at other degrees of freedom, you can also explore the demo here: https://rpsychologist.com/d3/tdist/ How do these different distributions compare to one another? What changes? What stays the same?

title: Lab 7: Introducing the t-statistic
Lab 7: Introducing the t-statistic
text:
Effect sizes
In addition to the statistical significance, it is always helpful to calculate a measure of effect size to get a sense of the practical significance of the effect. For a one-sample t-test, we can use the same measure of effect size that we had used previously, the Cohen’s d. Although we do not know our population standard deviation, σ, we can still use the same formula and interpretation with our sample standard deviation instead.
\[
d=\dfrac{M-\mu}{SD}
\]
Previously, we calculated Cohen’s d using the formula. This time, we’ll be using the effectsize package to help do this for us.
Let’s first install and load in the effectsize package.








Now that we have loaded in the effectsize package, we can use a function called cohens_d(). The syntax for this formula is quite similar to the one we just used for the t.test() function. We first provide the data column that we are working with, followed by the mu that we are comparing to – we do not need to provide an alternative parameter.
Fill in the code block below to find the Cohen’s d for our pref1 data.








How should we interpret this Cohen’s d value? What does this tell us about the practical significance of our result?

title: Lab 7: Introducing the t-statistic
text:
Confidence intervals
One other thing that you might have noticed is that the output our t.test() above also produces a confidence interval. This gives us an interval that is likely to contain the population mean, μ, with an associated level of confidence. Previously, we calculated our confidence interval by using the corresponding critical z-value: \[
CI=M \pm z_{crit}\times SE,\ where\  SE=\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}
\]
Notice here that we do not have our population standard deviation, σ. What we’ll do instead is estimate this using our sample standard deviation. Similarly, we will sub out our critical z-value with our critical t-value instead:
\[
CI=M \pm t_{crit}\times SE,\ where\  SE=\dfrac{SD}{\sqrt{n}}
\]
This confidence interval is interpreted in the exact same way as we had done previously. By default, the t.test() function will calculate a 95% confidence interval, but we can adjust our level of confidence by adjusting the conf.level parameter in our t.test() function.
Use the code block below to see what happens to our confidence interval when we change the associated confidence level to 99%.

title: Lab 7: Introducing the t-statistic
text:
Reporting our results
The last important step in our NHST procedure is to actually report our results. To do so, we’ll be using the guidelines provided by the American Psychological Association (i.e., APA style/format), just like we had done previously when reporting our descriptive statistics. A few elements we need to include reporting our results are:

What statistical test we used
Descriptive statistics for our data (e.g., mean, standard deviation, confidence interval)
The calculated test statistic (t), degrees of freedom (df), and p-value
The effect size (d) and interpretation.
If our findings are significant, we also want to report the direction of this difference (e.g., which group was bigger or smaller?)

Oftentimes, the calculated test statistic, degrees of freedom, p-value, and effect size are reported together at the end of the sentence, with values reported to two or three decimal places. As an example, we could report the findings of our analysis like:

“A one-sample t-test was used to determine whether the the proportion of gaze to the singer of the familiar song at the baseline phase differed from that expected by chance (0.5). There was no significant difference in the proportion of time spent looking at the person singing the familiar song at baseline (M = 0.52, SD = 0.18, 95% CI [0.46, 0.58]) from chance, t(31) = 0.67, p = 0.51, d = 0.12. This was a very small effect.”







TipActivity 2



In the above analysis, we found that the proportion of gaze to the singer of the familiar song at the baseline phase did not differ from what we would expect by chance. However, there was also a second test phase where the researchers measured the proportion of gaze after each singer sang a familiar or unfamiliar song. This data can be found in the pref2 column. Adapt the code above to use the one-sample t-test to see whether we seen any differences after the singers sang their song. Use a two-tailed test with an α = .05. Calculate the associated effect size and a 95% confidence interval. Make sure to report your findings using APA style.

title: Lab 5: Sampling Distributions, the Central Limit Theorem, and Hypothesis Testing
text:
In this lab, we’ll start to explore how we can use data from a sample to make claims about its associated population. Before starting this lab, make sure to have read Chapter 5: Sampling, the Central Limit Theorem, and Hypothesis Testing from your textbook.






NoteLearning objectives



By the end of this lab, you should be able to:

Define what a sampling distribution is, particularly the distribution of sample menas
Define what the central limit theorem is, particularly in reference to the mean, standard deviation, and shape of the distribution of sample means
Describe how changing the sample size affects the distribution of sample means
Define, interpret and use R to calculate standard errors
Describe why the central limit theorem is important in statistics, particularly in null hypothesis significance testing (NHST)
Use R to conduct and interpret a z-test

title: Lab 5: Sampling Distributions, the Central Limit Theorem, and Hypothesis Testing
text:
Population parameters and sample statistics
As psychologists, we are almost always interested in drawing conclusions about a population, or a very large group of people (e.g., all undergraduate students in Canada, all Canadians, all human beings, etc.). Despite this, we are almost always working with a sample (e.g., participants in a study) because it would not possible to get data on every single person in our population.
As an example, let’s imagine that we are working with IQ scores. These are designed so that at the population level, the distribution of scores is normal with a mean IQ score of 100 and a standard deviation of 15. These values are referred to as population parameters because these are characteristics of the population. Population parameters are oftentimes denoted by using lowercase Greek letters, with μ (mu) being used for population means and σ (sigma) being used for population standard deviations.
For our example, let’s imagine that we are interested in IQ scores for the entire population of the fictional city of Springfield. Before we start, let’s first run the code below to prep us for the lab1.








Next, let’s set up and visualize the IQ scores for the underlying population of 1,000,000 people in Springfield. Do not worry if you don’t understand all the code below. As an important note, remember that we practically NEVER actually observe this!








Let’s then imagine that we are working with Professor Frink, the local scientist in Springfield, to run a study where we are have participants complete an IQ test. Let’s compare the mean IQ scores after we collect two samples, one with 5 and one with 100.



Here, we’ll use the slice_sample() function, which let’s us randomly select a number of rows from our dataset.








These mean values that we just calculated are referred to as sample statistics since these are properties of our sample data. The first thing to note is that both of these are pretty close to our population mean of 100 – this makes intuitive sense because these samples are collected to approximate our population. The other thing to note is that our second sample is closer to our actual population mean. This is a demonstration of the law of large numbers, which says that more observations gives us a better approximation of the true average.
Regardless, in either case, we don’t get the exact population parameter of 100. In fact, there will always be some degree of imprecision between our sample statistic and our population parameter, which is referred to as sampling error. This sampling error can be exacerbated if we have some form of sampling bias when we are selecting our participants, but will occur naturally even if we have a perfectly representative sample.

title: Lab 5: Sampling Distributions, the Central Limit Theorem, and Hypothesis Testing
text:
Sampling distributions
If it’s the case that we will always encounter some form of sampling error, then how do confidently make inferences about our population? To explore how we are able to do so, let’s imagine that we decide to replicate our study. In other words, we will obtain a random sample of 5 people and have them complete our IQ test. We will then do this again and again and again, replicating our study 5,000 times.
Run the code below to see what happens when we replicate our study. Don’t worry about understanding the nuts and bolts of the code. We’ll then look at the first few replications.








In the table above, we can see that each row corresponds to the results of one of our replications, with each column being the score of a given participant. Each time we run our study, we calculate a new sample_mean. As we noted before, this sample mean will always be a little bit off of our population parameter of μ = 100. However, notice what happens when we plot the results of each of the values in our sample_mean column.
We’ll make a histogram that visualizes all of the values in our sample_mean column, which takes the mean of each of our replications.








What can we take away from this image? What we see is that our sample_mean for a given replication tends to be between 80 and 120. What this means is that sometimes we’ll get a sample that happens to have a lower average IQ score (around 80) and other times, we’ll get a sample that happens to have a high average IQ score (around 120). However, for the most part, we see that the scores form a normal distribution centered around a mean of 100 – in other words, our population mean! As we mentioned earlier, increasing our sample size gives us a better estimate of what our population parameter is.
Let’s see what happens when we repeat the same process, but this time, we’ll obtain a random sample of 100 people instead of 5.








How does this histogram compare to the one we created earlier? In both cases, we see that our scores again form a normal distribution centered around a mean of 100. However, because we are getting a better estimate, notice that our scores are more tightly clustered around this mean – rather than ranging from 80 and 120, our distribution now ranges between 95 and 105.
The histograms that we just plotted shows a special kind of distribution, called the distribution of sample means. This is a theoretical distribution of our sample means if we were to obtain every single possible sample of a given size2. The reason this is theoretical is because it would be impossible to obtain every single possible sample. Nonetheless, we can understand what the distribution of sample means will look like due to one of the most important theorems in statistics…

The tidyverse is a collection of packages that share a common way of thinking and working with data, which provides a more modern workflow for using R. title: Lab 3: Describing Data
text:
In this lab, we’ll be using R to help us describe the data that we are working with. Before starting this lab, make sure to have read Chapter 3: Middle-ish: Describing the Middle and Spread of Your Data from your textbook.






NoteLearning objectives



By the end of this lab, you should be able to:

Use R to calculate different measures of central tendency (mean, median, mode)
Identify scenarios when each measure of central tendency would be most appropriate to use
Use R to calculate different measures of variability (range, interquartile range, standard deviation, variance)
Identify scenarios when each measure of variability would be most appropriate to use
Report descriptive statistics using APA formatting

title: Lab 3: Describing Data
text:
Mean
Let’s start off with the mean, which is what we tend to think of when we imagine an “average”. This is a popular and commonly used measure of central tendency, which is computed by adding up the value of all of your data points and then dividing by the total number of data points that you are working with. In mathematical notation, this can be expressed as:
\[
M=\dfrac{\Sigma X}{n}
\]
Breaking down this formula a bit:

\(M\)typically denotes the mean.
\(X\)refers to the total set of data that we are working with.
\(\Sigma\) is the Greek capital letter sigma, which tells you to calculate the sum. Here, when we see \(\Sigma X\), this tells us to calculate the sum of \(X\), or all of the data points that we are working with.
\(n\) refers to the number of data points in the sample that we are working with. In the context of psychology research, this oftentimes refers to the sample size, or the total number of people in our sample.

Let’s try it for ourselves! We can use two functions: sum() to sum the values of a set of data, and length() to count up the number of values in a set of data. Let’s use these to calculate the mean of my_numbers :








Although it’s pretty straightforward to calculate the mean like this, there’s an even easier way to do so, the mean() function!
Let’s use the mean() function to calculate the mean of my_numbers instead:

title: Lab 3: Describing Data
text:
Median
Another common measure of central tendency is the median, which corresponds to the middle value of your set of data. To compute this, we list the values in order and then find the middle number of the list.

If we have an odd number of data points, there will be a single middle number that corresponds to our median. For example, the median of the numbers below would be 3: \[1,2,\textbf{3},4,5\]
If we have an even number of data points, there will be two middle numbers. In this case, we take the mean of those numbers. For example, the median of the numbers below would be 3.5:
\[1,2,\textbf{3,4},5,6\]

Let’s try it for ourselves! We’ll use the sort() function to sort my_numbers so that we can then find the median:








After sorting the list, it’s relatively straightforward to find the median, especially since our data is fairly small. Once we are working with lots of numbers, this gets fairly tedious. Fortunately, there is a median() function to help compute this for us.
Let’s use the median() function to calculate the median of my_numbers instead:

title: Lab 3: Describing Data
text:
Mode
The last common measure of central tendency is the mode, which tells you the most frequently occurring value in your data. Unlike the mean and median, R does not actually have a preset function to calculate the mode for us (there is actually a mode() function, but it does something completely different). However, we did learn a tool to quickly glean how frequent each value appears in our dataset: the frequency table. As a quick reminder, we used the dplyr package to help us make some nice looking frequency tables last time, but we can make a quick-and-dirty version of this using the table() function instead.
Let’s use the table() function to help us identify the mode of my_numbers:








Note that you can have multiple modes in your dataset if there are multiple values that are most common (sometimes referred to as bimodal if there are two modes, or multimodal if there are even more). Also note that this means that sometimes the mode may not be informative, such as when all values are equally as common (e.g., a uniform distribution).

title: Lab 3: Describing Data
text:
Which measure should we use?
The mean, median, and mode all provide a measure of central tendency, but each do so in a different way. Knowing how to calculate each is helpful, but understanding when to use each and what they imply is critical for accurately describing your data. For example, let’s look at the scenario below to see how each of these measures can be affected by our data.






TipActivity 1



Let’s see how the mean and median change when we change our data. list1 and list2 below have the same data, except for the last number. Fill in the blank with whatever number you want and see how the corresponding mean and median change. You can try this as many times as you want – just press the Start Over button and run the code again. What happens when you put in a very small number? What about a very big number?










As you’ll find with most things in statistics, there aren’t necessarily hard and fast rules for when to use each of these different measures. However, you can use the following as a rough guideline as you are deciding what measure of central tendency would be most appropriate for a given set of data:

If you are working with nominal data, you should be using the mode (e.g., how would you calculate the mean or median for a nominal variable like eye colour?) Even if your nominal data are represented as numbers, both the mean and median assume that the numbers in your data are meaningful, so these will be uninterpretable if the numbers are arbitrarily assigned.
If you are working with ordinal data, you most likely want to use the median instead of the mean. The median requires that you have some sort of meaningful order to your data, but does not depend on the precise numbers involved – however, this is important when calculating the mean, so it is less appropriate when working with ordinal data.
If you are working with interval or ratio data, the mean is usually a good default since many statistical tools are based on the mean and lots of people know what it is. However, as we saw earlier, the mean is susceptible to outliers, or extreme scores in our dataset. This can be particularly noticeable if you have some sort of skew in your dataset, where the mean gets pulled in the direction of the extreme scores. In these scenarios, the median likely provides a better definition of where the center of your data is. This is also why it is important to first explore and visualize your data to get a rough idea of the data that you are working with.

title: Lab 3: Describing Data
text:
Range
The most straightforward measure of variability is the range, which is the biggest value minus the smallest value. When looking at my_numbers, the biggest (or maximum) value is 15 and the smallest (or minimum) value is 6, so we can calculate the range by subtracting these two.
Let’s use the max() and min() functions to help us calculate the range of my_numbers:








Alternatively, we can use the range() function:








Although the range is straightforward measure of variability, it is oftentimes not the most nuanced. Since it only relies on two data points, it is especially susceptible to outliers in our data. For example, think back to the earlier activity comparing the means and medians for list1 and list2 – what are the ranges of these lists?

title: Lab 3: Describing Data
Lab 3: Describing Data
text:
Standard deviation and variance
Another way to think about describing the variability in the data is to calculate the standard deviation (SD). Like how the mean is the most commonly reported measure of central tendency, the standard deviation is the most commonly reported measure of variability. The general premise of the standard deviation is to tell us the average (i.e., standard) distance that your points tend to be from the mean (i.e., deviation). If this number is large, that means that many of our data points are far away from the middle, so our distribution is spread out. On the other hand, if this number is small, that means that many of our data points are close to the middle, so our distribution is clustered together.
To make this a bit more concrete, let’s apply this to our list of my_numbers. Previously, we found the mean of our list to be \(M=9.86\). We can first see how far each of our scores are from that mean value by taking the difference between the value and the mean (\(X-M\)):

We can then take the average, or mean, of these deviations to give us a measure of variability. When calculating the mean, the first step is to sum() up all the values, so let’s try this first:








Hmm… there seems to be a problem since our sum of deviations is pretty much 01. This will always be the case since positive deviations from the mean will cancel out with negative deviations from the mean. One way in which we can get around this issue is to square all of our deviations, which makes everything a positive number. We can then sum up these squared deviation values to then calculate this average deviation – this sum has its own term: the sum of squares. Going back to our my_numbers, this would look something like:

\(\Sigma(X-M)=0\)
\(\Sigma(X-M)^{2}=46.86\)



Now that we have a sum, we just need to divide by the number of scores that we are working with to calculate a mean. One notable difference is here is that we will be dividing by \(n-1\) instead. The reason we do this is a bit nuanced, but we will revisit this later on later on in this course. In doing this, we are calculating a measure of variability called the variance. We can also calculate the variance using the function var() that goes through this whole process for us.
Let’s try calculating our variance of my_numbers, both by calculating the sum of squares and finding the “average”, and by using the var() function:








The variance is a helpful measure of variability, but it is hard to interpret what it actually means since all of the differences are squared. Although this has some nice mathematical properties, descriptive statistics are ultimately meant to describe data! This is where the standard deviation comes in. This solves the problem in a rather straightforward way – we take the square root of the variance to put things back into their original units. Just like the variance, we can also calculate the standard deviation with the sd() function.
Let’s try calculating the standard deviation of my_numbers. We can take the square root of the variance we calculated earlier using the sqrt() function, and compare this to the sd() function.








In practice, we typically just calculate the standard deviation using software, but it is helpful to know what the underlying computations involved are. This whole process that we walked through can be summarized with the standard deviation formula here:
\[
SD=\sqrt{\dfrac{\Sigma(X-M)^{2}}{n-1}}
\]
Although it looks a bit intimidating at first, we are ultimately trying to find the average distance a data point strays from the center:

First, we calculate all the deviations by looking at the difference between each point and the mean (i.e., \(X-M\))
If we try to add this up, we will always get 0 because the positive and negative deviations will cancel out
To get around this, we square each of our deviations to make all the numbers positive and sum this up instead, giving us our sum of squares (i.e., \(\Sigma(X-M)^{2}\))
To find an average, we’ll divide by the number of points we’re working with. Due to some properties of working with a sample, we divide by \(n-1\) instead. This leaves us with our variance
The variance tells us the average squared deviation, which is a bit difficult to interpret. To put everything in the original units, we square root our variance, finally giving us the standard deviation

title: Lab 1: Introduction to R + Exploring Data
text:
Comments and commands
You might notice that in each of the code blocks above, the first line did not seem to do anything. These first lines are called comments. Comments are sections of code that we leave to help other humans read and understand the code later on, but are intended to be ignored by computers. In R, we will use the # symbol to denote that something is a comment. In other words, any line that starts with a # will be considered a comment and ignored, and any line that does not start with a # will be considered a command and run.
In practice, comments are used all the time to communicate with others who are trying to use the code. This includes describing the purpose of a chunk of code, what options are available to change, etc. You should get in the habit of using comments since oftentimes, the other person you are helping is yourself in the future. If you want to write a longer comment, it is a good idea to put a # at the beginning of multiple lines.
Let’s try this for ourselves! You can click into the window below and try typing whatever you want after a line that begins with a #. Afterwards, run the code in the window and see what happens.








Notice that running this code did not anything since each line began with a # so it was ignored.

title: Lab 1: Introduction to R + Exploring Data
text:
Objects
One of the most important things we can do R (or any other programming language) is to store information in an object. You can think of an object like a box that you can store anything in—a number, a message, a dataset, a plot, etc. The value of an object is whatever you put inside this box, and the name is whatever name you end up calling it so that both you and the computer can refer to it later on.
To create an object, we will need to use an assignment operator, which allows us to assign a value to an object name. In R, the assignment operator looks like an arrow: <-
Let’s try it for ourselves! We will go through a simple example to show how this is done.








We can then use this object later on to reference the information stored in it. What do you think the output of the code below will be?








A few important things to note about objects! You can name your objects anything you want, but there are a few rules that you need to follow:

R is case-sensitive, so any little change in the name of an object will be considered a separate object (e.g., “favourite_number” is different than “Favourite_number”.
You can use letters, numbers, underscores, and periods for your name, but they must always start with a letter.
Names need to all be in one word (i.e., no spaces).

Lastly, it’s important to remember that the order in which you run R code is very important. R code is evaluated in order, from the top of the page to the bottom. Objects created first will be stored for later on, but you can only access it once it has been created. If you are trying to access an object at the bottom of the page before creating it earlier on, this will result in an error. In addition, you can overwrite the value in an object if you assign a new value to an existing object later on.






TipActivity 1



Let’s try assigning a new value to the favourite_number object. What do you think will happen when we subtract 2 from favourite_number now?

title: Lab 1: Introduction to R + Exploring Data
text:
Functions
So far, we’ve used simple operators to do basic arithmetic and assign values to objects. Oftentimes, we will want to do more complex things. In these cases, we will use what is called a function. Functions compute an operation, but are not limited to what individual symbols mean (in fact, operators are just special kinds of functions). If we are thinking about R as a language, we can think of functions like verbs and objects like nouns.
We’ve already come across a function at the beginning of this lab: print("Hello, world!").
We can think of functions as having three basic parts:

The first part is the name of the function (e.g., print)
The second part is what you are putting into the function, or the arguments (e.g., "Hello, world!"). Sometimes a function can take more than one argument, separated by commas. Each function is unique in what it can do and what arguments it uses. We will learn about some other useful functions as we progress throughout the course.
The last part is the output of the function, which is whatever results from the corresponding operation.







TipActivity 2



Here, we will try out a new function called sum() to add up all the numbers in it. sum() is an example of a function that takes multiple arguments. Let’s use it to add up the numbers 5, 10, and 15.

title: Lab 1: Introduction to R + Exploring Data
text:
Errors
R is a very flexible language that allows you to do literally thousands of different things. That being said, it is quite picky, which means that you are going to encounter an error eventually. Get comfortable with seeing errors, because everyone, even the most experienced coders, will have errors with their code at first. When this happens, consider this to be a “first draft” of your code which you can then refine until your code does what you want.
Figuring out why your code has an error is a big part of programming. You will oftentimes not be the first one to run into a certain error message, so you can usually solve this by:

Searching the internet. You can typically find your answer if you copy and paste your error message into Google. You will usually come across examples where other have encountered the same problem and looked for help. StackOverflow is a website that can be particularly helpful since it collates answers based on how useful others found it.
Asking somebody in the real-world: You can also show your code to a friend (e.g., someone else in the course, your TA, or Dr. Hong) to see if they have any advice when you get stuck.
A note on generative AI. It is getting increasingly common for people to use generative AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Copilot) to get help while coding. You will likely receive some helpful guidance here by asking what you did wrong, but these answers are not always reliable. These tools can generate plausible, but incorrect and/or misleading, information, and it is necessary to build the knowledge and skills to evaluate their responses. Since this course is an introductory course, it is recommended that you avoid getting help from generative AI tools as you are building up your foundations.

title: Lab 2: Visualizing Data
text:
In this lab, we’ll be using R to help us visualize data. Before starting this lab, make sure to have read Chapter 2: Using Graphs to Visualize Data from your textbook.






NoteLearning objectives



By the end of this lab, you should be able to:

Describe what packages in R are
Recognize the initial steps of exploring, preparing, and visualizing data
Use dplyr() to create frequency tables
Use ggplot() to create different types of graphs (bar graphs, histograms, and scatterplots)
Apply best practices for creating graphs
Visually describe the shape of a distribution

title: Lab 2: Visualizing Data
text:
Packages
Before we get started, we will have to learn about packages (or libraries). When you first install R onto your computer, you’ll have access to many basic functions like print() and sum(). However, other users in the R coding community are always writing and distributing new functions for the rest of the world to use. You can kind of think of this like downloading new DLC content to expand what you can do in a video game (except it is freely available!) In R, these collections of functions for download are called packages. Rather than having to re-invent the wheel and re-write code from scratch each time we want to do something new, we can load in functions already contained within these accessible packages instead.
Installing new packages into your R environment is a two-step process:

First, you need to download and install them onto your computer, typically using the function install.packages().
Secondly, you need to actually load the package so that you can use it in your current code, using the function library().

Today, we’ll be installing and using two packages. dplyr (pronounced “dee-ply-er”) contains a few different functions that are helpful for preparing and organizing data, and ggplot2 (usually referred to us just “gee-gee-plot”) contains functions that can help us make all sorts of different graphs.
Run the code in the window below to install and load in the dplyr and ggplot2 packages. Note that you might get some warning messages here, but that should be OK!














Important



When working with R, you will need to load in the packages each time you use them. Since we are using R online, this means that you will need to re-install and re-load these packages each time you refresh the page.

title: Lab 2: Visualizing Data
Lab 2: Visualizing Data
text:
Bar graphs
For our first graph, let’s compare the frequencies of each Education level and plot it as a bar graph, which helps us compare values across categories. For our bar graph, our key components will be:

Data: The NHANES dataset we are working with. Like with our frequency tables, we’ll re-order the levels to make it a bit more intuitive to read.
Aesthetics: We’ll map our different Education levels onto the x-axis (horizontal).
Geometry: Since we’re creating a bar graph, we will use the geom_bar() function. This will automatically calculate the frequencies and map it onto the y-axis (vertical).

Let’s put this altogether to make our bar graph.








Great, we just made our first bar graph! Note that we had seen this data being presented both as a frequency table and as a bar graph. Depending on what you are using it for, you may opt to use one or the other. One thing that you might have noticed is that ggplot uses a + to add on additional layers instead of the pipe (|>) we used earlier.
Sometimes, a figure like this is sufficient as we are first exploring data for ourselves. However, when we are sharing figures with others, we want to make it easier to interpret for others. Let’s add some additional layers to customize our plot a bit.

Firstly, you might notice that our axes labels are a bit uninformative. It’s always a good idea to give your graph informative titles and labels to help readers better interpret them.
Additionally, when creating data visualizations, it is usually a good idea to minimize the visual clutter to help your data better show through.
That being said, there’s a lot room for creativity in your figures, as long as you’re communicating your findings effectively, ethically, and efficiently.

Here, we’ll add a title and labels to our graph with the labs() function. We’ll also clean up our graph a bit using the theme_minimal() function. Last, we’ll add a color by adding a fill argument to our geom_bar() function.

title: Lab 2: Visualizing Data
text:
Scatterplots
Now that we know how ggplot2 works, we can apply this same idea to make other types of graphs. We create a scatterplot to explore the relationship between different continuous variables. In this example, let’s look at the relationship between Weight and Height in our dataset. Many of the steps involved will be the same:

Data: Just like before, we’ll use our NHANES dataset. Note that we will not need to re-order our levels because we are working with two continuous variables.
Aesthetics: Here, we need to specify which variable will be on our x-axis and which will be on our y-axis. In this case, we’ll put Weight on our x-axis and Height on our y-axis.
Geometry: To create a scatterplot, we’ll use the geom_point() function to plot each participant as a datapoint.
Just like before, we’ll customize our plot a bit to add titles and axes labels, and minimize visual clutter.

Let’s use the code below to make a scatterplot to visualize the relationship between Weight and Height.

text:
Histograms
The last graph that we’ll cover today is a histogram. Although a histogram looks quite a bit like a bar graph, it helps us to visualize continuous, rather than categorical data. This is particularly helpful in showing us the distribution of a given variable. Using the same general idea as before, let’s use a histogram to visualize the distribution of our Height variable.
This time, we’ll use the geom_histogram() function to make a histogram for our Height variable.

text:
Other types of graphs
Although we’ve only covered a few of the basic graphs in this lab, you can use the same general principles to create a whole host of different graphs. For example, you can use the geom_violin() function to make violin plots, geom_density() to make density plots, geom_jitter() to make jitter plots, and so on! title: Lab 4: z-scores, Normal Distributions, and Probability
text:
In this lab, we’ll be using R to help us start working with z-scores, normal distributions and probabilities. Before starting this lab, make sure to have read Chapter 4: z Scores: Data Distributions, the Normal Curve, and Probability from your textbook.






NoteLearning objectives



By the end of this lab, you should be able to:

Define, interpret and use R to calculate z-scores
Understand the basic properties of the normal distribution
Understand how z-scores relate to properties of the normal distribution
Interpret and use R to compute probabilities of events within the context of a normal distribution

title: Lab 4: z-scores, Normal Distributions, and Probability
text:
Calculating z-scores
To calculate a z-score, we can use the following formula:
\[
z=\dfrac{X-M}{SD}
\]
In plain language, we’ll first take the difference of our raw score and the mean (\(X-M\)). Afterwards, we’ll divide this results by our standard deviation (\(SD\)). The resulting value is the z-score that corresponds to your given raw score.
For this example, let’s load in sample-class.csv, a made-up dataset with class test scores in different courses.








We can then use the mean() and sd() functions to help us calculate the z-score corresponding to our grade of 85 relative to the other CogPsych_Exam and the SocPsych_Exam scores:

title: Lab 4: z-scores, Normal Distributions, and Probability
text:
Interpreting z-scores
How should we interpet these z-scores? We can compare the sign and the size of the numbers:

The sign (i.e., positive or negative) of a z-score tells us whether our score is above or below the mean. In this case, our grade of 85 is above the mean in our Cognitive Psychology course, but below the mean in our Social Psychology course.
The size (i.e., absolute value) of a z-score tells us the distance from the mean, in the units of standard deviations. The larger the value, the further away a score is from the mean. In this case, our grade of 85 is over 2 standard deviations above the mean in our Cognitive Psychology course, but close to 0 standard deviations below the mean in our Social Psychology course.

title: Lab 4: z-scores, Normal Distributions, and Probability
section: Converting between z-scores and raw scores
text:
Converting between z-scores and raw scores
Using some algebra to rearrange our z-score formula, we can also derive a formula to calculate a raw score from a z-score:
\[ z=\dfrac{X-M}{SD} \]
\[ z \times SD={X-M} \]
\[ X = z \times SD+M \]
In other words, if we know what the z-score is within a given distribution, we can find the original score.
Let’s find the raw score that corresponds to a z-score of 1.5 on our CogPsych_Exam grades.

title: Lab 4: z-scores, Normal Distributions, and Probability
text:
Standardizing scores
Lastly, we can convert all of our grades to their corresponding z-scores, or standardize our scores, using the scale() function. This is especially helpful when we don’t yet have a good idea of how to interpret a variable and its measurement. In addition, this helps us to identify potential outliers in our data.
As a brief aside, we previously used the $ symbol to access variables in our dataset. However, we can also use the $ to create new variables in our data.
Let’s use the scale() function to convert each of the grades to their corresponding z-score, which we can then store in a new variable.








Importantly, when we are standardizing our data, all we are doing is re-labelling our scores, NOT re-positioning them. In doing so, we change some of the characteristics of our dataset:

The new mean becomes 0, providing a convenient reference point
The new standard deviation becomes 1, providing a standard unit of comparison
The new shape is the same as it was originally. If the original distribution was normal, the standardized distribution will be normal. Likewise, if the original distribution was skewed, the standardized distribution will still be skewed.







TipActivity 1



Let’s use ggplot2 to create a few histograms to help us visualize how our original and standardized distributions compare to one another. Fill in the blanks below to first create a histogram of the original scores (e.g., CogPsych_Exam, SocPsych_Exam, or DevPsych_Exam). Then compare this to the histogram of the standardized scores (e.g., CogPsych_Exam_z, SocPsych_Exam_z, or DevPsych_Exam_z). What stays the same? What changes?

title: Lab 6: Effect Sizes and Confidence Intervals
text:
In this lab, we’ll use R to start working with effect sizes and confidence intervals. Before starting this lab, make sure to have read Chapter 6: Effect Sizes and Confidence Intervals from your textbook.






NoteLearning objectives



By the end of this lab, you should be able to:

Understand the outcomes and limitations of null hypothesis significance testing (NHST)
Define and differentiate between Type I (false positive) and Type II (false negative) errors
Define, interpret and use R to calculate Cohen’s d, as a measure of effect size
Define, interpret and use R to calculate confidence intervals

title: Lab 6: Effect Sizes and Confidence Intervals
Lab 6: Effect Sizes and Confidence Intervals
Lab 6: Effect Sizes and Confidence Intervals
text:
Calculating a confidence interval
So how do we calculate a confidence interval? Let’s say that we want to calculate the 95% confidence interval for IQ scores after participating in our study program. As a starting point, we will use our sample mean, \(M=108\). We know that this will not be exactly the same as our population mean, μ. However, from the central limit theorem, we know that the distribution of sample means that this comes from will be normally distributed. Because of this, we already have the basis for calculating an interval for where 95% of scores will fall between!






CautionRecap




In a normal distribution, how many standard deviations will 95% of the scores fall within? Hint: you can use the qnorm() function in the code block below or alternatively, you can look this up using your unit normal table. These should be the positive and negative versions of the same number.











From the central limit theorem, what is the standard deviation of our distribution of sample means?






The range of our confidence interval can thus be calculated using the equation below. Here, \(z_{crit}\) corresponds to the z value associated with our selected confidence level. Note that we are actually calculating two values here, since we have an upper and lower bound to our interval.
\[
CI=M \pm z_{crit}\times SE,\ where\  SE=\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}
\]
Let’s calculate the 95% confidence interval for IQ scores after taking part in our new study program. This will be based on our sample of \(n=25\) participants who had an average IQ score of \(M=108\) after completing our study program. IQ scores are normally distributed in the population with a \(\mu=100\) and \(\sigma=15\).








Based on this, we are 95% confident that the mean IQ score after undergoing the study program falls between 108 ± 5.88, which 102.12 and 113.881. To report this according to APA guidelines, we first state the confidence level that we are using, followed by our lower and upper bounds separated by a comma in square brackets. This is oftentimes reported with our other descriptive statistics. In our example, we could say report our confidence interval as “The mean IQ score after taking part in the study program was M = 108 (95% CI [102.12, 113.88]).”






TipActivity 2



Now you try! Use the code blocks below to calculate the 99% confidence interval for IQ scores after participating in our study program?



What is the \(z_{crit}\) value that corresponds to a confidence level of 99%? You can use the qnorm() function in the code block below or alternatively, you can look this up using your unit normal table. As a friendly reminder, it is always helpful to draw the associated curve to help you visualize what you are looking for. The response below should be a positive number











What is the standard error?











Use the se object you just created to calculate the lower bound of the 99% confidence interval. You can round the \(z_{crit}\) value to two decimal places.











Use the se object you just created to calculate the upper bound of the 99% confidence interval. You can round the \(z_{crit}\) value to two decimal places.











Based on your calculations, what is the 99% confidence interval? How does this compare to your 95% confidence interval? How would you report this according to APA guidelines?

title: Lab 6: Effect Sizes and Confidence Intervals
text:
Footnotes


As a sidebar, many people (even those who use confidence intervals all the time!) will oftentimes interpret a confidence interval to mean that there is “a 95% probability that the true mean lies inside this range”. This makes intuitive sense since it aligns with the common sense idea of being “95% confident”. However, what our confidence interval really tells us is that if we were to conduct this same study over and over and over again, 95% of our calculated confidence intervals would contain the true population mean. To see this in practice, you can visit the visualization here: https://rpsychologist.com/d3/ci/↩︎
